REPLY BRIEF
No one defends Stinson v. United States, 508 U.S. 36
(1993), as written.  It is a relic of a different era —a
time when th e Court presumed that Congress had
impliedly delegated to every agency authority to
interpret its own rules, and when the Court  treated
those interpretations as binding unless “plainly
erroneous.”  Bowles v. Seminole Rock & Sand Co., 325
U.S. 410, 414 (1945).  In Stinson, this Court extended
that deference doctrine —known as Seminole Rock
deference—to the U.S. Sentencing Commission, and
adopted verbatim Seminole Rock ’s statement of the
rule for deference.  508 U.S. at 45.
That deference standard conflicts with this Court’s
recent decisions.  In Kisor v. Wilkie, 588 U.S. 558 (2019),
members of this Court disagreed about whether to
limit Seminole Rock deference or overrule it, but all
rejected its “reflexive” deference standard.  588 U.S. at
574 (citation omitted); id.  at 623 (Gorsuch, J.); id.  at
632 (Kavanaugh, J.).  In Loper Bright Enterprises v.
Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), the Court went
further:  It rejected the theory that Congress impliedly
delegated to agencies the power to interpret statutes—
a “fiction” that conflicted with the “elemental proposi -
tion” that “courts decide legal questions by applying
their own judgment.”  Id. at 391-392, 404.
In light of those decisions, the court -appointed
amicus curiae offers no defense of Stinson ’s central
premise—that Congress impliedly delegated to the
Commission the power to interpret the Guidelines
through commentary.  Instead, amicus tries (Br. 18) to
locate some “express” basis for Stinson ’s deference
standard, so that this Court might preserve in
criminal sentencing a form of reflexive deference that
it has repudiated for every other administrative body.

2

There is no basis—express or implied—for that anomalous result.  Under the Sentencing Reform Act of
1984 (SRA), Pub. L. No. 98-473, Tit. II, Ch. II, 98 Stat.
1987, district courts must determine the appro priate
“sentencing range” for an offense by interpreting  and
applying the “guidelines,” 18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(4) (emphasis added)—not the Commission’s “official commenta -
ry,” or even its “policy statements,” 18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(5),
(b).  When a court calculates the applicable sentencing
range, there is no room for deference to the Commis -
sion, no matter what form its interpretation takes.
If the Court retains Stinson ’s “caricature” of
Seminole Rock deference (on amicus’s new theory or
any other), it would require courts to defer even when
a Guideline is not “genuinely ambiguous.”  Kisor, 588
U.S. at 574.  It would require courts to defer without
carefully considering the Guideline’s “text, structure,
history, and purpose”; to defer because the Guideline
seems “impenetrable on first read.”  Id . at 575.   To
affirm the court below, the Court would need to em -
brace an approach that “commentary controls even
unambiguous guidelines.”  United States v. Vargas, 74
F.4th 673, 682 (5th Cir. 2023) (en banc).  That cannot
be right.
For its part, the government maintains (Br. 18 -22)
that Seminole Rock deference should still apply, albeit
within the limits set forth in Kisor.  The government
is right that Stinson ’s “plainly erroneous” standard
cannot stand.  But the government disclaims Stinson’s
standard in name, only to embrace it in practice.  In
the government’s view (Br. 22-26), “ambiguity” in the
Guidelines will “not be uncommon,” and deference will
be “frequently,” “necessarily,” or “ ‘by definition’ ” appropriate.  The Commission’s commentary, it says, offers
a “shortcut” for provisions that “  ‘make the eyes glaze
over.’ ”  Id. at 24 (quoting Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575).

3

This Court has repeatedly disclaimed such reflexive
deference, and it should not retreat here.  When courts
interpret guidelines, they should do so with no
deference to the commentary.  At minimum, courts
cannot defer to commentary without observing Kisor’s
limits.  Because the court of appeals held otherwise,
the Court should vacate the judgment below and
remand so that the court of appeals may consider in
the first instance the proper interpretation of U.S.S.G.
2K2.1(a)(3).
I. THE SENTENCING REFORM ACT DOES
NOT EXPRESSLY DELEGATE TO THE
COMMISSION AUTHORITY TO
INTERPRET GUIDELINES
Every federal criminal sentencing begins the same
way:  District courts must properly interpret the
“guidelines” to calculate the appropriate “sentencing
range.”  See 18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(4).  Courts of appeals
review that interpretation de novo  to determine
whether the sentence “was imposed as a result of an
incorrect application of the sentencing guidelines.”
18 U.S.C. 3742(a)(2).  When courts interpret the
guidelines, they consider a “legal question.”  Loper
Bright, 603 U.S. at 392.  Unless Congress expressly
directs otherwise, they  must do so according to their
“own judgment.”  Ibid.
Consistent with Loper Bright , amicus accepts (Br.
25-32) that deference to the Commission must come
from an express delegation.  Amicus therefore strains
to find a statutory hook for deference.  None exists .
Deference to commentary conflicts with the SRA’s text
and structure and poses constitutional concerns.

4

A. The Commission’s Authority To Issue
Policy Statements Does Not Support
Deference To Commentary
Amicus principally contends (Br. 18 -25) that the
Commission issues commentary under its authority to
promulgate “general policy statements.”  28 U.S.C.
994(a)(2).  From there, amicus maintains (Br. 25- 29)
that the SRA expressly authorized the Commission to
interpret the Guidelines through policy statements,
and that such interpretations control unless “plainly
erroneous.”
Every step of that argument is wrong.  “Commentary”
is not a “policy statement.”  The Act does not delegate
to the Commission authority to interpret Guidelines
through policy statements.  And even if it did, that
delegation would not trigger the reflexive deference
set forth in Stinson.
1. The Commission’s “commentary” is distinct
from the “policy statements” it issues
Amicus’s argument fails at the threshold:  interpretive commentary is not an exercise of the Commission’s
authority to issue policy statements.
The SRA contemplates that the Commission will
issue three kinds of text.  First, the Commission may
promulgate “guidelines,” for use “in determining the
sentence to be imposed in a criminal case.”  28 U.S.C.
994(a)(1).  Second, it may issue “general policy
statements regarding application of the guidelines. ”
28 U.S.C. 994(a)(2).  Stinson addressed a “third variant
of text”: “commentary.”  508 U.S. at 41.  Although the
Act did not authorize commentary in “express terms,”
the Commission has appended “commentary” to the
Guidelines since the first Guidelines Manual.  Ibid.;
see Pet. Br. 5.  And Congress later amended the Act to

5

recognize “official commentary.”  Pub. L. No. 100-182,
§ 3, 101 Stat. 1266.
Section 3553 expressly distinguishes these three
categories and assigns each a different role at
sentencing.  Section 3553(a)(4) requires district courts
to consider the applicable “sentencing range” for the
defendant “as set forth in the guidelines.”  18 U.S.C.
3553(a)(4).  Separately, courts must consider at
sentencing “any pertinent policy statement.”  18 U.S.C.
3553(a)(5).  Section 3553(b)(1) expressly distinguishes
“official commentary,” and assigns it a different role:
When the Guidelines were mandat ory, courts could
consider the Commission’s “official commentary,”
alongside “sentencing guidelines” and “policy state -
ments,” to determine which departures were permissible.
18 U.S.C. 3553(b)(1); see 18 U.S.C. 3553(b)(2). Those
“different terms”—distinguished within the very same
provision—must be given different meanings.  Mohamad
v. Palestinian Authority, 566 U.S. 449, 456 (2012).
The Commission’s practice draws the same line.
Throughout the Guidelines Manual, it designates
some provisions “policy statements” and others
“commentary” or “application notes,” and it observes
that division section by section.  “Policy statements”
are labeled as such and occupy their own numbered
sections of the Manual, in place of individual
Guidelines. See, e.g., U.S.S.G. 1B1.10, 1B1.11, 1B1.12,
1B1.13, 3F1.1, 5D1.4, 5E1.5, 5F1.7, 5J1.1, 5K1.1,
5K1.2, chs. 6 & 7, 8D1.4, 8F1.1.  “Commentary” is a
different class of text, U .S.S.G. 1B1.7, set off
by its own heading and appended to Guidelines
and (tellingly) policy statements.  The Commission’s
consistent, decades -long practice belies any notion
that it intended “commentary” to serve as a “policy
statement.”

6

Contra amicus (Br. 19), the Commission has not
purported to treat all commentary as an exercise of
its policy statement authority.  Until Stinson , the
Commission instructed courts to treat its interpretive
commentary “much like legislative history.”  508 U.S.
at 46 (quoting U.S.S.G. 1B1.7, comment. (1992)).  And
until 2025, Section 1B1.7 distinguished between
commentary that “interpret[s] the guideline” and
commentary that “may suggest circumstances which,
in the view of the Commission, may warrant departure
from the guidelines.”  U.S.S.G. 1B1.7 (2024).  Section
1B1.7 specified only that the  latter class of
commentary should “be treated as the legal equivalent
of a policy statement,” i bid., consistent with the role
that Section 3553(b) assigned to such commentary.1
Nor is “commentary” a mere “label,” as amicus
maintains (Br. 19 -20).  Administrative law has long
distinguished a “general statement[] of policy” from an
“interpretive rule.” See Am. Hosp. Ass’n v. Bowen ,
834 F.2d 1037, 1045- 1046 (D.C. Cir. 1987).  An
interpretive rule states “ ‘what [an] administrative
officer thinks the statute or regulation means ’ ”—it
is “an agency attempt to give meaning ” to a
term.  Id.  at 1045 (citation omitted) .  A general


1 In 2025, the Commission amended Section 1B1.7 to delete the
instruction to treat even departure -related commentary as the
“legal equivalent of a policy statement.”  U.S.S.G. App. C, amend.
836 (Nov. 1, 2025).   It did not alter  the commentary to Section
1B1.7, which states that portions of the document not labeled as
guidelines or commentary “are to be construed as commentary
and thus have the force of policy statements.”  U.S.S.G. 1B1.7 ,
comment.  Because the pre -amendment text of Section 1B1.7
treated only commentary addressing departures as the “legal
equivalent of a policy statement,” the commentary to that
provision is best read the same way.

7

statement of policy is different: I t announces the
agency’s “intentions for the future.”  Pacific Gas & Elec.
Co. v. FPC , 506 F .2d 33, 38 (D.C. Cir. 1974).
Commentary construing a term in a Guideline does
the paradigmatic work of an interpretive rule.
That is true of the commentary at issue here.
Application Note 2 to Section 2K2.1 appears immedi -
ately beneath a header entitled “Commentary.”
U.S.S.G. 2K2.1, comment. (n.2).  The commentary is
interpretive:  It defines a phrase (“large capacity
magazine”) that appears in the Guideline itself.  Ibid.
That is not a policy statement; it is an interpretation
of the Guideline’s text.
2. Congress did not expressly delegate to the
Commission the authority to interpret
Guidelines through policy statements
Even if commentary could be recast as policy
statements, reflexive deference to interpretive policy
statements—no less than to interpretive commentary—
conflicts with the SRA’s text and structure and raises
constitutional concerns.
a.  The Act provides no textual basis for deference to
policy statements, just as it provides none for
deference to commentary.  See Pet. Br. 15-18.  Section
994(a)(2) authorizes “general policy statements regarding
application of the guidelines.”  28 U.S.C. 994(a)(2).
That authorizes the Commission to state its general
views about how the Guidelines should be implemented and to advise courts on the exercise of
sentencing discretion.  It is not authority to declare,
with controlling force, what Guidelines mean.
In its essentials, the Act is akin to  the
Administrative Procedure Act.  The Commission
promulgates “guidelines,” which must go through

8

notice-and-comment and congressional review, 28
U.S.C. 994(a)(1), (p), (x), just as an agency’s legislative
rule must, 5 U.S.C. 553.  And the Commission may
issue “policy statements” or “official commentary”
exempt from those procedures, 28 U.S.C. 994(a)(2); 18
U.S.C. 3553(b)(1), just as administrative agencies may
issue “general statements of policy” or “interpretative
rules,” 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A).
No one understands the APA to contain an express
delegation of binding interpretive authority .  When an
agency interprets its own regulations, deference is
rooted in an implied delegation —a “presumption that
Congress would generally want the agency to play the
primary role in resolving regulatory ambiguities.”
Kisor, 588 U.S. at 569  (plurality opinion) .  Were
the APA’s reference to “ interpretative rule[s]” or
“statements of policy ” an express delegation to issue
authoritative interpretations of regulations, there
would be no need for that presumption.
This Court demands more for an express
delegation—Congress must assign “an agency the
authority to give meaning to a particular . . . term. ”
Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 394.  The Secretary of Labor,
for instance, may expressly “define[] and delimit[] by
regulations” certain statutory terms for purposes of
the minimum-wage provisions.  Id.  at 395 n.5 (citing
29 U.S.C. 213(a)(15)).  The Nuclear Regu latory
Commission may “define[] by regulation s” what it
means for a defect in a nuclear facility to “create a
substantial safety hazard.”  Id. at 395 n.5 (quoting 42
U.S.C. 5846(a)(2)).  And the Sentencing Commission
was expressly charged with “describ[ing] what should
be considered extraordinary and compelling reasons
for sentence reduction” under 18 U.S.C. 3582(c)(1)(A).
28 U.S.C. 994(t); see Rutherford v. United States, 146 S.

9

Ct. 1320, 1334 (2026).  Section 994(a)(2) stands in stark
contrast:  It authorizes the Commission to issue policy
statements only “regarding application” of the guide -
lines, not to “define[],” “delimit[],” or even “describe”
any term—let alone all terms—in the Guidelines.
b.  Reflexive deference to commentary would also
conflict with the structure of the SRA, regardless of
whether the Commission issues commentary under its
authority to promulgate policy statements.  The
Commission must follow rigorous procedures before
promulgating Guidelines, but policy statements (like
commentary) are not subject to these safeguards.  See
Pet. Br. 19-20.  The Commission must afford Congress
a 180- day window to review and potentially reject
amendments to “guidelines,” but not policy statements.
28 U.S.C. 994(p).  And amendments to “guidelines” —
but not policy statements —must undergo notice-andcomment rulemaking.  28 U.S.C. 994(x).
Amicus responds (Br. 39) that the Commission, in
practice, often puts commentary (and policy state -
ments) through the notice-and-comment process.  That
misses the point.  The Congress that insisted on
congressional oversight and public input when the
Commission promulgated (then-mandatory) Guidelines
would not have handed the Commission so easy a
means of circumventing those safeguards.  Congress’s
choice to exempt commentary (and policy statements)
from the notice- and-comment process confirms that
interpretations found in those texts were never meant
to bind courts.
c.  Deference to commentary—whether or not issued
as a “policy statement”—also implicates grave constitutional problems.  First, binding deference would give
the Commission the final word on interpretive
questions, encroaching on the judicial power.  See Pet.

10

Br. 22.  Amicus responds (Br. 33 -34) that Guidelines
lack the force of law after United States v. Booker, 543
U.S. 220, 245 (2005).  But even after Booker, the proper
interpretation of Guidelines remains a question o f  l aw.
Courts must still determine the meaning of a
Guideline to calculate the applicable sentencing range,
18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(4), and courts of appeals must do so
on review, 18 U.S.C. 3742(f)(1); see Gall v. United States,
552 U.S. 38, 50 (2007).  Consistent with Article III,
courts must “decide [those] legal questions by applying
their own judgment.”  Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 392.
In addition, deference would allow the Commission
to exercise legislative power over criminal punishment
without congressional oversight.  See Pet. Br. 22.  The
Guidelines, though no longer binding, still serve as the
“benchmark” for every criminal sentence, and courts
may vary from them only for reasons “sufficiently
compelling” to support the degree of variance.  Gall ,
552 U.S. at 49- 50; Pet. Br. 4.  The Guidelines thus
“anchor” criminal sentences for tens of thousands of
individuals each year.  Peugh v. United States, 569 U.S.
530, 549 (2013).  That is a considerable power, and one
that must be subject to congressional review.
d.  This Court’s decision in Williams v. United States,
503 U.S. 193 (1992), does not change matters.  Cf.
Amicus Br. 19.  In Williams, the Court considered
whether a sentencing court could depart on a ground
that a policy statement expressly forbade.  503 U.S. at
199-200.  At the time, Section 3553(b) prohibited
departures unless the Commission had not adequately
considered a circumstance “in formulating the
guidelines.”  Id.  at 198 (quoting 18 U.S.C. 3553(b)
(1988)).  The holding in Williams  follows from that
provision:  The Commission cannot have failed to

11

consider a circumstance that it “expressly rejected” “as
an appropriate ground for departure.”  Id. at 200.
Williams does not suggest, however, that a policy
statement is binding any time it interprets a term in
the Guidelines.  The Court had no occasion to
announce such a rule, because the policy statement
before it did nothing of the sort.  In any event, Kisor
and Loper Bright foreclose a reading of Williams that
would require reflexive deference to an interpretive
policy statement.  The Commission has no authority to
bind courts to its interpretation of the Guidelines,
whether it speaks through commentary or a policy
statement.
3. Even an express delegation would not
justify Stinson’s form of reflexive deference
In all events, amicus’s “express delegation” theory
would not salvage Stinson ’s formulation of the
deference standard, let alone the Fifth Circuit’s
approach, under which commentary controls  even
unambiguous Guidelines.  See Vargas, 74 F.4th at 682.
At most, it would provide a textual hook for Seminole
Rock deference, as refined by Kisor.
Whether Congress delegates interpretive authority
expressly or by implication, there is no call for
deference unless the court encounters ambiguity.
Otherwise, the Guideline “just means what it means—
and the court must give it effect” when it calculates the
sentencing range.  Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575.  Put
differently, if the Guideline “gives an answer,” “then a
court has no business deferring to any other reading.”
Ibid.  Thus, even if Congress expressly delegated
authority to interpret the Guideline, that would not
“permit the [Commission], under the guise of

12

interpreting a [Guideline], to create de facto  a new
[Guideline].”  See Christensen v. Harris Cty., 529 U.S.
576, 588 (2000); see also Rutherford, 146 S. Ct. at 1334
(“independently” interpreting a statute even where
Congress had expressly delegated to the Commission
authority to construe the statute’s terms).
At bottom, amicus advocates for a version of Stinson
that goes beyond even Seminole Rock .  He urges (Br.
32) this Court to reject ambiguity as the trigger for
deference.  But if ambiguity is not the trigger, that
leaves something worse:  A court must defer to
commentary even when it contradicts a Guideline that
is unambiguous under the ordinary tools of
construction.  See Vargas, 74 F.4th at 682.  That would
turn textual interpretation on its head:  “When the
words of a [provision] are unambiguous,” the “judicial
inquiry is complete.”  Conn. Nat’l Bank v. Germain, 503
U.S. 249, 254 (1992) (citation omitted).
B. The Commission’s Authority To Issue
Guidelines Does Not Support Deference
To Commentary
Finally, amicus presses an alternative (and bolder)
argument (Br. 39-46):  Commentary may be sustained
under the Commission’s authority to promulgate
“guidelines,” 28 U.S.C. 994(a)(1), at least where the
commentary underwent notice and comment and
congressional review.  That theory is not Stinson’s, and
it is unsound.
In Stinson, this Court held that commentary binds
even when it has not cleared the procedural hurdles
imposed on Guidelines.  508 U.S. at 45- 46.  Amicus’s
fallback position abandons that holding —it requires
“modif[ying]” Stinson to withdraw deference from any
commentary that does not satisfy Section 994’s

13

procedural requirements.  Amicus Br. 39, 41.  If
nothing else, this new theory cannot be defended on
the basis of stare decisis.
Amicus’s theory is also wrong on its own terms.
Guidelines and commentary differ as a matter of
statutory text and procedure, and neither the
Commission nor courts may reclassify one as the other
after the fact.  Section 3553, as explained, expressly
distinguishes between “guidelines,” “policy state -
ments,” and “official commentary,” and assigns each a
different role at sentencing.  18 U.S.C. 3553(a), (b) ;
see p. 5, supra.  Congress directed courts to “consider”
“guidelines” in calculating a “sentencing range,” 18
U.S.C. 3553(a)(4), but omitted “commentary” from that
directive, even as it included a reference to
“commentary” in the “very next provision,” Loughrin v.
United States, 573 U.S. 351, 358 (2014).   The natural
inference is that commentary occupies a distinct—and
subordinate—category, set apart from the Guidelines.
See Pet. Br. 16-17.
It is therefore beside the point whether “commentary”
undergoes notice-and-comment review or is submitted
to Congress.  Cf.  Amicus Br. 39 -46.  “Commentary”
does not become a “ guideline” simply because the
Commission chooses to send it down that procedural
path.  When a court interprets a “guideline” to properly
calculate the “sentencing range,” its task thus remains
the same—it must look to the text of the “guideline,”
not the “commentary.”  18 U.S.C. 3553(a)(4); 18 U.S.C.
3553(b)(1).
Amicus’s approach would also make sentencing
unadministrable. Before considering any piece of
commentary, a court would first need to reconstruct
whether the commentary in fact satisfied Sections
994(p)’s and 994(x)’s requirements.  Then, the court

14

would need to sort commentary by when it issued,
assigning at least the commentary issued before
Stinson the weight of “legislative history”—consistent
with the Commission’s original instructions.  See Pet.
Br. 6.  Finally, the court would be left the task of
applying Stinson:  deciding when a commentary’s
erroneous reading of the Guideline is “plain” enough to
escape deference.  508 U.S. at 45.
The simpler, and correct, approach is to let courts
interpret the Guidelines as they interpret any other
provision—according to their own best judgment.
II. THIS COURT SHOULD REJECT —OR AT
LEAST CAREFULLY LIMIT—DEFERENCE
BASED ON AN IMPLIED DELEGATION
OF INTERPRETIVE AUTHORITY
In Stinson, this Court did not locate any basis for
deference in the SRA’s text.  Instead, it adopted the
deference doctrine set forth in Seminole Rock, which is
rooted in a “presumption” that Congress intended to
delegate binding interpretive authority.  See Kisor, 588
U.S. at 569 (plurality opinion).  That approach is
wrong.  It “ conflict[s],” as amicus recognizes (Br. 15),
with this Court’s later decision in Loper Bright, which
rejected that kind of implied delegation as a “fiction.”
603 U.S. at 404.  Because Congress never expressly
delegated the power to create binding interpretive
commentary, see Part I, supra,  there should be no
deference at all.
The government nevertheless urges this Court to
afford the commentary a particularly robust form of
deference, Br. 22 -28, even as it states that Kisor
applies with “full force” to the Guidelines, Br. 29.  That
approach is wrong, too.  Whether this Court rejects
Stinson’s implied delegation outright (consistent
with Loper Bright ), or  simply reinforces the limits

15

inherent in the doctrine (consistent with Kisor), the
result is much the same:  Deference is inappropriate.
1.  To start, deference is incompatible with the
criminal setting.  See Abramski v. United States, 573
U.S. 169, 191 (2014); see Pet. Br. 24-28.  Before a court
affords Seminole Rock deference, it must consider the
“character and context” of the interpretation at issue .
Kisor, 588 U.S. at 576.  The “context” when interpreting
a Guideline is criminal sentencing, where deference to
an agency “can result not just in added regulatory
burdens, but in the loss of liberty during months or
years of extra prison time.”  NAFD Br. 9.  The “elemental
proposition” that courts must “apply[] their own
judgment,” Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 392, is never more
important than when an individual’s liberty is at stake.
In response, amicus understates the Guidelines’
“real and pervasive effect” on criminal sentencing.
Molina-Martinez v. United States, 578 U.S. 189, 199
(2016).  The Guidelines “anchor” the defendant’s
sentence.  Id. at 198-199 (citation omitted).  A district
court cannot vary from the Guidelines unless it
explains the variance with specificity, see Peugh, 569
U.S. at 542-544; 18 U.S.C. 3553(c)(2), and considers
the need to avoid unwarranted disparities, 18 U.S.C.
3553(a)(6).  Thus, commentary that makes the
Guideline more punitive has the “purpose and effect”
of “increas[ing] the rates and length of incarceration.”
Peugh, 569 U.S. at 545 (citation omitted).  That
“context” calls for a “strong judicial role,” not deference.
Kisor, 588 U.S. at 576, 580.
2.  Even when applying Seminole Rock deference,
courts may defer to an agency’s interpretation of its
own regulation only in the face of genuine ambiguity,
and only after exhausting the traditional tools of
construction.  Kisor, 588 U.S. at 574-575.  When a court

16

applies those tools , it “will resolve many seeming
ambiguities out of the box, without resort to [Seminole
Rock] deference.”  Id. at 575.
The government resists that approach, maintaining
that courts may use commentary as a “shortcut” when
interpreting a Guideline that is “impenetrable on first
read.”  Br. 24 (quoting Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575).  This
Court has held otherwise:  Text that “make[s] the eyes
glaze over” gives a court no license to “wave the
ambiguity flag.”  Kisor, 588 U.S. at 575.  A court must
always “carefully consider[] the text, structure, history,
and purpose of a [Guideline], in all the ways it would
if it had no [commentary] to fall back on.”  Ibid.  When
a c ourt does so, “instances of genuine guideline
ambiguity” should indeed be “uncommon.” Cf. U.S. Br.
24; Kisor, 588 U.S. at 632 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring
in the judgment).
And if genuine ambiguity remains, the answer is to
resolve it in the defendant’s favor, not to defer to
commentary.  Bifulco v. United States , 447 U.S. 381,
387 (1980); Pet. Br. 24-26.  The rule of lenity promotes
a substantive preference for liberty, and the Guidelines,
while advisory, Amicus Br. 33-38, substantially influence
prison sentences.  See  United States v. Bass, 404 U.S.
336, 348 (1971).  Lenity also promotes fair notice.
Although this Court has held that due process does not
require fair notice of Guideline provisions, Beckles v.
United States , 580 U.S. 256,  266, 267 (2017),
predictability in criminal sentencing remains an
expectation of Congress, see 28 U.S.C. 994(x); 28 U.S.C.
991(b)(1)(B); cf. Fed. R. Crim. P. 11(b)(1)(M).  In all
events, the Guidelines became advisory only because
this Court in Booker excised the provisions that made
them mandatory.  543 U.S. at 245 -259.  Nothing in
Booker, however, purported to alter how courts

17

construe the Guidelines, whether then in existence or
issued since.  See id. at 264; NAFD Br. 14.
3.  In addition, the ordinary justifications for deference will rarely —if ever—apply to the Commission’s
interpretation of the Guidelines.  See Pet. Br. 29-33;
NAFD Br. 9-24.
First, the Commission has no “comparative exper -
tise” in interpreting Guidelines.  Kisor, 588 U.S. at 578.
The government maintains otherwise but relies on
the Commission’s expertise in setting “sentencing
polic[y].”  U.S. Br. 26 (quoting 28 U.S.C. 991(b)(1))
(emphasis added).  That is not expertise in resolving
legal questions. As this Court explained in Loper
Bright, an agency’s subject -matter expertise gives it
“no special competence” in construing a legal text.  603
U.S. at 400-401.  That observation applies with parti -
cular force to the Guidelines, which use common legal
terms that district courts encounter during senten -
cings “every day.”  Id. at 401; see Pet. Br. 29-30, 41-42.
Second, the Commission’s role in drafting the
commentary offers no basis for deference.  Cf. U.S. Br.
23 (quoting Stinson, 508 U.S. at 45).  Commentary may
issue “well after the guideline it interprets ha[s] been
promulgated.”  508 U.S. at 44.  More fundamentally, a
court interpreting a Guideline should seek its objective
meaning—the understanding a reasonable reader
would draw from the text —not its drafters’ “actual
intent.”  FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital
Master Fund, Ltd., 608 U.S. 608, 621 n.5 (2026).
Finally, binding commentary is not needed to
achieve uniformity among the lower courts.  Cf.  U.S.
Br. 24 -25.  If the Commission can identify and
eliminate ambiguity through commentary, it can do so
in the text.  So if litigation reveals ambiguities

18

regarding the meaning of a Guideline,  Section 994(o)
provides the solution —the regular, annual cycle of
Guideline amendments, 28 U.S.C. 994(o) , subject to
public comment and congressional review.  And if the
Sentencing Commission “anticipates ambiguities in
the guideline text ,” the path is even more
straightforward:  It can “preemptively address[] them”
through the text of the Guideline itself.  U.S. Br. 25.
*  *  *
None of this means that c ourts must construe
Guidelines in a vacuum or disregard commentary
entirely.  Cf.  Amicus Br. 4.  Courts may credit
commentary to the extent it persuades —the same
“respect” that thorough and well -reasoned guidance
has always earned.  Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S.
134, 140 (1944); see Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 385-386.
Courts may also consult commentary where it
illustrates the operation of a technical rule, provided
that it does not change the rule’s substance.  What
courts may not do is substitute the Commission’s
interpretation of the Guideline for their own judgment
as to the text’s single, best meaning.
III. STARE DECISIS DOES NOT PREVENT THIS
COURT FROM REVIS ITING STINSON’S
DEFERENCE STANDARD
Even as amicus disclaims Stinson ’s reasoning, he
invokes (Br. 47-51) stare decisis to save its deference
standard.  Stare decisis, however, does not require this
Court to retain Stinson ’s deference standard, and
certainly does not require it to disregard the limits in
Seminole Rock deference identified in Kisor.
1.  This Court need not run through the stare decisis
factors to discard Stinson’s deference standard.  It has

19

not hesitated to reject adherence to a “doctrinal
dinosaur or legal last-man-standing.”  Nat’l Republican
Senatorial Comm. v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404, 2424 (2026)
(citation omitted).  In those circumstances, the Court
has described its “hollowed -out precedents as ‘so
undermined’ by subsequent developments that they
are ‘no longer good law’ and ‘retai[n] no vitality.’ ”  Ibid.
(citation omitted).
That is Stinson.  The decision rested on an implied
delegation to create binding interpretive commentary—
a theory that amicus does not defend given Loper
Bright.  But even as amicus disavows Seminole Rock
deference, he would leave behind its vestiges —its
“classic formulation” of the deference standard—for
the Sentencing Commission alone.  Kisor, 588 U.S. at
574.  Stare decisis is no cause for that odd result.  Loper
Bright and Kisor have already hollowed out Stinson’s
reasoning; discarding Stinson ’s statement of the
deference standard only “formalize[s] what is evident”
from those decisions.  Herrera v. Wyoming , 587 U.S.
329, 342 (2019).
2. “If anything more is left of  ” Stinson’s deference
standard, this Court should overrule it.  Trump v.
Slaughter, 146 S. Ct. 2283, 2302 (2026) (emphasis
omitted).  Stare decisis—even were it “enhanced”
(Amicus Br. 47)—does not counsel otherwise, just as it
did not save the deference doctrine set forth  in
Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense
Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984).
The Court’s reasoning in Stinson  has “eroded ”
beyond repair.  United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506,
521 (1995).  Indeed, in light of this Court’s more recent
decisions, retaining Stinson ’s reflexive deference
standard would not serve the “evenhanded, predict -
able, and consistent development of legal principles.”

20

Gamble v. United States , 587 U.S. 678, 691 (2019)
(citation omitted).  Rather, it would conflict with Loper
Bright’s instruction that legal provisions have a
“single, best meaning,” not a range of “permissible”
alternative constructions.  603 U.S. at 400.  It would
also conflict with Kisor, which disclaimed the “plainly
erroneous” test as a “caricature” of the doctrine.  588
U.S. at 574.
Stinson, moreover, does not provide a workable rule.
As amicus emphasizes (Br. 4, 20, 21, 49), the doctrine
requires a court to disregard commentary in plain
conflict with the Guideline.  But if courts struggle to
reach consensus as to whether language is genuinely
ambiguous, see Amicus Br. 3, it will prove no easier to
distinguish between “flat inconsistency” and mere
inconsistency.  Stinson, 508 U.S. at 43.  If courts are not
to exhaust the interpretive toolkit before deference,
when should they stop?  After a quick review of the
text?  A glance at the structure?  Applying some (but
not all) canons of construction?  Now that Kisor has
awoken courts “from [a] slumber of reflexive
deference” in administrative law, the Court should not
reinforce that deference  in criminal sentencing.
United States v. Nasir, 17 F.4th 459, 472 (3d Cir. 2021)
(en banc) (Bibas, J., concurring).
Conversely, there is nothing disruptive about
eliminating Stinson’s deference standard.  Where the
commentary reflects the best reading of the Guideline,
courts will follow it.  Where it does not, the
Commission can move the commentary to the text,
after congressional review and public oversight.
Indeed, the Commission  has already begun the
process.  Pet. Br. 44-45.  If any remaining commentary

21

cannot survive without deference, it will be abrogated
for good reason.2
3.  If  this Court retains any deference, it must at
least enforce Kisor’s limits.  Stare decisis was no
obstacle in Kisor to reinforcing the limits in Seminole
Rock deference, 588 U.S. at 574, and it is no obstacle
here either.
And once this Court recognizes the “inherent” limits
to Seminole Rock , Kisor, 588 U.S. at 574, the Court
need only follow them to their conclusion:  There can
be no deference, at least to commentary, like that  at
issue here, that makes the text more punitive.  For the
reasons explained, deference is ill -suited to the
criminal context, conflicts with the rule of lenity, and
contravenes the other ordinary justifications for
deference.  See pp. 15-17, supra.  Rather than force
lower courts to reach that conclusion as to Guideline
after Guideline, this Court should confirm as much
categorically.
Doing so would not require the Court to jettison
the result in Stinson  itself:  That case concerned
commentary narrowing the scope of a sentencing
enhancement, 508 U.S. at 39, so deference did not
conflict with the rule of lenity or the principles that
animate it.  The Court, however, need not “extend
[Stinson] to the limits of its logic.”  Hein v. Freedom
From Religion Foundation, Inc. , 551 U.S. 587, 615
(2007) (plurality opinion).  There is no reason for

2 Amicus (Br. 51) worries that abrogating deference could
prompt a “flood” of claims on collateral review.  “[E]very circuit to
‘look[ ] at the issue, ’ ” however, “ ‘has agreed that a defendant
cannot use a § 2255 motion to vindicate non -constitutional
challenges to advisory guideline calculations.’ ” Bullard v. United
States, 937 F.3d 654, 660-661 (6th Cir. 2019) (citation omitted)
(collecting cases).

22

deference where, as here, the commentary increases
the harshness of a guideline.
IV. THIS COURT SHOULD VACATE THE
JUDGMENT BELOW AND REMAND
The government agrees (Br. 3, 28-29) that the Court
should vacate the decision below and remand. The
court of appeals should have the opportunity to
interpret Section 2K 2.1 without deference to the
commentary.  See Pet. App. A2; J.A. 18.
The government maintains (Br. 31 -32) that it will
win on remand, but —as it recognizes—its arguments
are properly directed to the court of appeals (or the
district court) in the first instance.  In any event, the
government is wrong.  Section 2K 2.1’s enhancement
applies only to offenses involving a “semiautomatic
firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity
magazine.” U.S.S.G. 2K2.1(a)(3).  As explained in the
opening brief (at 45 -47), that text cannot cover
petitioner’s offense involving a Glock 17, perhaps the
country’s most ubiquitous firearm.  That is plainly true
without deference, and it is true under Kisor, too:  The
text is unambiguous and, even if it were  not, this
commentary would not warrant deference.  See NAFD
Br. 23-24.
The government questions (Br. 31) whether the
court of appeals will revisit circuit precedent when
interpreting Section 2K2.1 on remand.  But if this
Court rejects or cabins deference, its decision would be
an intervening development that would “relieve[]” the
court of appeals of its duty to follow circuit precedent
under the “rule of orderliness.”  Sandoval Argueta v.
Bondi, 137 F.4th 265, 271 (5th Cir. 2025).  Regardless
of whether that will be true of every precedent relying
on Stinson deference, see ibid. (reserving the question

23

after Loper Bright ), it must at least be true of the
specific precedent that is under review in this case.
Finally, the government highlights the district
court’s statement that it “would have imposed the
same sentence” even if the range were miscalculated.
Br. 32 (quoting J.A. 21).  In the Fifth Circuit, however,
it is “not enough for the district court to say  the same
sentence would have been imposed but for the error.”
United States v. Tanksley, 848 F.3d 347, 353 (5th Cir.),
supplemented, 854 F.3d 284 (5th Cir. 2017).  That kind
of boilerplate statement is common —some district
courts in the Fifth Circuit make it  in virtually every
case—and the court of appeals often remands in spite
of such assurances.  See, e.g., United States v. Ritchey,
117 F.4th 762, 767-768 (5th Cir. 2024); United States v.
Taylor, 2022 WL 2752602, at *2 (5th Cir. July 14, 2022)
(per curiam); Tanksley, 848 F.3d at 353; United States
v. Martinez-Romero, 817 F.3d 917, 925, 926 (5th Cir.
2016) (per curiam).  And on remand, “district courts
often impose lighter sentences when confronted with a
sentencing error no matter how emphatically they
indicate[d] otherwise.”  United States v. Redmond, 965
F.3d 416, 421 (5th Cir. 2020).  The courts below should
have the opportunity to follow the same course here.

24

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons and those stated in the
opening brief, the judgment below  should be vacated
and the case remanded for further proceedings.
